extracted.intended_audience: playwrights, screenwriters, fiction writers, and students of dramatic/creative writing
extracted.subtask_description: Guidelines for constructing plays and stories emphasizing a clear thematic premise and character-driven plotting; includes Egri's prescriptions for character traits, motivations, dialectical structure, and conflict resolution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Premise (thematic truth)
rubrics_metrics.description: Central to Egri's argument is his claim that the best stories follow the logical method of thesis, antithesis, synthesis, or dialectic, to prove what he calls a 'premise'. A premise, as Egri describes it, is a thematic truth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a single, clear premise (thematic truth) to drive the whole play/story. Egri's example: 'stinginess leads to ruin'—from this statement the writer can detect the beginning (establish an obsessively stingy character), middle (collision with inevitable opposition), and end (the character's ruin). The premise suggests the logical course of events and should be the organizing idea behind plot choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character drives plot (character over plot)
rubrics_metrics.description: Egri argues against Aristotle's view of character being secondary to plot. According to Egri, well-defined characters will drive the plot themselves, and so the foundation of character is the essential germination of a well crafted story.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build plot consequences from characters' internal traits and decisions rather than forcing characters to fit a predesigned sequence of events. Anti-pattern: starting with a plot gimmick and shoehorning characters into it; instead, allow characters' compulsions to generate the action.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dialectical structure (thesis—antithesis—synthesis)
rubrics_metrics.description: Stories should follow the logical method of thesis, antithesis, synthesis (dialectic) to prove the premise.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Structure scenes and acts so that an initial assertion (thesis) is opposed by conflicting forces (antithesis), producing a synthesis (resolution) that demonstrates the premise. Use the dialectic to map beginning, middle, and end tied to the thematic claim.

rubrics_metrics.name: Begin with characters, not events
rubrics_metrics.description: Creative writing should start from identification of one or more main characters, rather than from actions, events, or incidents.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose and define main character(s) first; let their traits and goals suggest the plot. Avoid the opposite approach of plotting set-pieces first and creating characters to service them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Overriding trait / 'compulsion' as dramatic engine
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should have an overriding trait (Egri’s word is 'compulsion'), typically negative, such as greed, snobbery or extravagance, coupled with the determination that that trait should prevail.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Give protagonists/antagonists a single dominant compulsion that drives their choices. Make that compulsion visible in behavior and choices to create consistent motivation and predictable conflict. Example traits: greed, jealousy, pride.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand characters' motivations; supply histories/biographies
rubrics_metrics.description: The author should clearly understand his characters’ motivations, if necessary by providing histories/biographies which inform the story even if they do not form part of it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Develop backstory and psychological detail for characters so motivations are coherent and plausible on the page; these biographies can remain off-stage but must inform decisions and dialogue. Anti-pattern: vague, unexplained motives that make behavior feel arbitrary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two-opposing-flaws structure (satisfying structure)
rubrics_metrics.description: A satisfying structure—used in many of the book's examples—is one in which two characters with opposing flaws are inextricably bound together, leading to a crisis in which the conflict is resolved by some dramatic action.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create paired characters whose opposing compulsions naturally bring them into conflict; bind them by circumstance so the clash culminates in a decisive crisis and an enacted resolution. This yields clear dramatic stakes and a convincing outcome tied to the premise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Emphasize change as dramatic necessity
rubrics_metrics.description: Egri emphasizes the ever-present role of change in all forms of life, forcing people to evolve and synthesize new philosophies in the face of one overwhelming obstacle after another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use external obstacles and conflicts to force characters to confront their compulsions and synthesize new perspectives (even if core traits remain). Change—incremental or situational—serves as the engine of dramatic progression.

rubrics_metrics.name: View of human motivation: selfishness / need for importance
rubrics_metrics.description: Egri claims 'All human beings are fundamentally selfish, their primary drive being to feel, or be perceived as, important.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Model character motivations around the desire for importance or self-regard to create believable drives; use this as a foundation when inventing goals, stakes, and conflicts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character consistency / fixedness
rubrics_metrics.description: Egri asserts that 'Human character is fixed and does not change significantly over life.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat core character traits as stable; dramatic interest comes from how situations reveal, test, or punish those fixed traits rather than wholesale personality transformations. Note: this is Egri's theoretical stance and may conflict with other approaches that favor transformative arcs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicability of method across forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Beyond the theater, Egri's methods have also been used to write short stories, novels, and screenplays.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adapt the premise/character-driven and dialectical principles to prose and screen forms—start with character, define a controlling premise, and structure conflicts so the thematic truth is demonstrated in action.
